subject: AI & Agents
title: Decision Trees: If-Then Intelligence
description: One-minute skill: Decision Trees: If-Then Intelligence.

hook.text: Is income > $50K? Yes → Is age > 30? Yes → Approve loan. A tree of questions makes the decision.

buildup.text: Decision trees split data by asking the most informative question at each step.

discovery.text: They're intuitive — you can literally draw the decision process and explain it to anyone.

twist.text: Single trees overfit easily. Random forests fix this by averaging hundreds of trees together.

climax.text: Gradient-boosted trees (XGBoost, LightGBM) dominate tabular data competitions to this day.

punchline.text: Sometimes the best AI is a really good game of 20 questions.

quiz.question: Why are random forests better than single decision trees?

details.summary: Decision trees make predictions by asking a series of yes/no questions, splitting data at each step until reaching a final prediction. They are simple, interpretable, and effective for structured data.
details.whyItMatters: Decision trees are one of the most interpretable models — you can trace exactly why a prediction was made. When explainability matters, trees offer transparency that neural networks cannot.
takeaways: Decision trees split data through a series of binary questions
They are highly interpretable — you can trace the reasoning
Random forests combine many trees for better accuracy

faq.question: How does a decision tree decide which questions to ask?
faq.answer: The algorithm finds the question that best separates the data at each step, using measures like information gain or Gini impurity. It picks the feature and threshold that create the purest possible splits.

faq.question: When should you use decision trees over neural networks?
faq.answer: Use decision trees when interpretability is important, data is structured and tabular, datasets are small, or you need to explain decisions to regulators. Neural networks are better for images, text, and very large datasets.
